claim: Copy number alterations (CNAs) play an important role in molding the genomes of breast cancers.
source: Copy number alterations (CNAs) play an important role in molding the genomes of breast cancers and have been shown to be clinically useful for prognostic and therapeutic purposes.
evidence: This is a general statement about the role of CNAs in breast cancer, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: CNAs have been shown to be clinically useful for prognostic and therapeutic purposes.
source: Copy number alterations (CNAs) play an important role in molding the genomes of breast cancers and have been shown to be clinically useful for prognostic and therapeutic purposes.
evidence: This statement references established clinical utility of CNAs, drawing from prior research in the field.

claim: Our knowledge of intra-tumoral genetic heterogeneity of copy number alterations is limited.
source: However, our knowledge of intra-tumoral genetic heterogeneity of this important class of somatic alterations is limited.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field, based on the authors' review of existing literature.

claim: Single-cell sequencing was used to comprehensively map copy number alteration heterogeneity in a cohort of breast cancer tumors.
source: Here, using single-cell sequencing, we comprehensively map out the facets of copy number alteration heterogeneity in a cohort of breast cancer tumors.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, which is detailed in the Methods section.

claim: The analyses reveal genetic heterogeneity of non-tumor cells (i.e. stroma) within the tumor mass.
source: Ou/var/www/html/elife/12-05-2020/backup/r analyses reveal: genetic heterogeneity of non-tumor cells (i.e. stroma) within the tumor mass
evidence: This finding is supported by the single-cell sequencing data presented in Figure 1 and related analyses.

claim: Copy number heterogeneity impacts breast cancer genomes, with the importance of both genomic location and dosage of sub-clonal events.
source: the extent to which copy number heterogeneity impacts breast cancer genomes and the importance of both the genomic location and dosage of sub-clonal events
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 2 and related analyses showing varying levels of heterogeneity and dosage effects.

claim: Genetic heterogeneity of chromosomal amplifications is pervasive in nature.
source: the pervasive nature of genetic heterogeneity of chromosomal amplifications
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 3 showing multiple forms of amplicon heterogeneity across samples.

claim: Copy number heterogeneity is associated with polyploidy.
source: the association of copy number heterogeneity with clinical and biological parameters such as polyploidy and estrogen receptor negative status
evidence: This association is demonstrated in Figure 5A with statistical testing (p-value=0.0164).

claim: Copy number heterogeneity is associated with estrogen receptor negative status.
source: the association of copy number heterogeneity with clinical and biological parameters such as polyploidy and estrogen receptor negative status
evidence: This association is demonstrated in Figure 5A with statistical testing (p-value=0.0229).

claim: Catalogues of recurrent driver alterations have been identified using an array of technologies.
source: Catalogues of recurrent driver alterations have been identified using an array of technologies (Teixeira et al., 2002; Adeyinka et al., 2003; Chin et al., 2006; Sjöblom et al., 2006; Fridlyand et al., 2006; Banerji et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Shah et al., 2012; Ciriello et al., 2015; Nik-Zainal et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Information about driver alterations has been instrumental in furthering understanding of breast cancer biology.
source: This information has been instrumental in furthering our understanding of the basic biology that underlies breast cancer development and has led to the development of diagnostic and prognostic tests and more importantly, the development of efficacious targeted therapies (Dawson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Disease relapse and therapeutic resistance remain important challenges in breast cancer treatment.
source: While the adoption of therapeutic strategies targeting somatic cancer alterations and the pathways they control has had a profound impact on the treatment of breast cancer (Alvarez et al., 2010), disease relapse and therapeutic resistance remain important challenges (Ma et al., 2015; Majewski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Genetic heterogeneity has been implicated as a common mechanism to explain recurrence and treatment failure.
source: Recent research into these phenomena has implicated genetic heterogeneity (i.e. sub-clonal variation or intra-tumoral heterogeneity) as a common mechanism to explain recurrence and treatment failure (Toy et al., 2013; Carey et al., 2016; Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent research.

claim: CNAs are an important class of somatic mutations acquired during breast cancer genome evolution.
source: CNAs are an important class of somatic mutations that are acquired during the evolution of breast cancer genomes (Dawson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The amplification of the ERBB2 (HER2) oncogene defines a biological subtype of breast cancers.
source: Most notably, the amplification of the ERBB2 (HER2) oncogene defines a biological subtype of breast cancers and targeting this CNA has led to the development of a multitude of efficacious therapeutic agents that have dramatically increased the survival of HER2+ patients (Arteaga and Engelman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents well-established knowledge in breast cancer biology.

claim: Targeting HER2 amplification has led to the development of efficacious therapeutic agents that have dramatically increased survival of HER2+ patients.
source: Most notably, the amplification of the ERBB2 (HER2) oncogene defines a biological subtype of breast cancers and targeting this CNA has led to the development of a multitude of efficacious therapeutic agents that have dramatically increased the survival of HER2+ patients (Arteaga and Engelman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents well-established clinical knowledge.

claim: Copy number information has utility in the prognostic stratification of breast tumors.
source: Additionally, numerous studies have demonstrated the utility of copy number information in the prognostic stratification of breast tumors (Russnes et al., 2010; Curtis et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Single-cell DNA sequencing methods have emerged as powerful tools for the study of intra-tumoral heterogeneity.
source: Single-cell DNA sequencing methods have recently emerged as powerful tools for the study of intra-tumoral heterogeneity with recent applications in breast (Navin et al., 2011; Eirew et al., 2015) and other tumors (Francis et al., 2014; Bolhaqueiro et al., 2019; Bian et al., 2018) revealing novel cancer genetics and biology.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research demonstrating the utility of single-cell sequencing.

claim: Samples from sixteen patients were selected from a cohort population enrolled in two phase II open-label clinical trials conducted by the Brown University Oncology Group (BrUOG).
source: Samples from sixteen patients were selected from a cohort population enrolled in two phase II open-label clinical trials conducted by the Brown University Oncology Group (BrUOG).
evidence: This describes the sample collection methodology for the study.

claim: Two pre-treatment, freshly frozen biopsies per patient were obtained.
source: Two pre-treatment, freshly frozen biopsies per patient were obtained.
evidence: This describes the sample collection methodology for the study.

claim: A mean of 116 single-nuclei per tumor sample were sequenced for a total of 2086 single-cell genomes.
source: A mean of 116 single-nuclei per tumor sample were sequenced in multiplex fashion for a total of 2086 single-cell genomes.
evidence: This describes the scale of sequencing performed in the study.

claim: Recurrent focal homozygous deletions on chromosomes 14 and 7 were observed in otherwise diploid genomes.
source: Intriguingly, we observed recurrent focal homozygous deletions on chromosomes 14 and 7, in otherwise diploid genomes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This observation is supported by the single-cell sequencing data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The deletions on chromosomes 14 and 7 localize to T-cell receptor alpha (TCRa) and beta (TCRb) loci.
source: Further inspection localized the deletions to T-cell receptor alpha (TCRa) and beta (TCRb) loci (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by detailed analysis of the deletion locations shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The TCR deletions are the result of T-cell maturation and generated via the process of V-D-J recombination.
source: These deletions are the result of T-cell maturation and generated via the process of V-D-J recombination.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of T-cell biology and the mechanism of TCR gene rearrangement.

claim: Focal homozygous deletions at the heavy and light Immunoglobulin loci (IGH and IGL) on chromosomes 14 and 22 denote B-cells.
source: Similarly, we observed focal homozygous deletions at the heavy and light Immunoglobulin loci (IGH and IGL) on chromosomes 14 and 22, respectively, denoting B-cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B and established knowledge of B-cell biology.

claim: The detection sensitivity of T-cells using single-nuclei copy number sequencing is approximately 80%.
source: Deletion analysis led to a calculated detection sensitivity of ~80% and 50% for T- and B-cells, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of purified T-cells where the expected deletion frequency was compared to observed frequency.

claim: The detection sensitivity of B-cells using single-nuclei copy number sequencing is approximately 50%.
source: Deletion analysis led to a calculated detection sensitivity of ~80% and 50% for T- and B-cells, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of purified B-cells where the expected deletion frequency was compared to observed frequency.

claim: T-cells were detected in almost all patient samples in varying proportions.
source: This allowed the quantification of T- and B-cells in the tumor mass in our samples and led to the detection of T-cells (in varying proportions) in almost all patient samples, with B-cell infiltration limited to a subset of tumors, (Figure 1C) consistent with previous studies (Ruffell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the quantification data shown in Figure 1C and is consistent with prior research.

claim: B-cell infiltration was limited to a subset of tumors.
source: This allowed the quantification of T- and B-cells in the tumor mass in our samples and led to the detection of T-cells (in varying proportions) in almost all patient samples, with B-cell infiltration limited to a subset of tumors, (Figure 1C) consistent with previous studies (Ruffell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the quantification data shown in Figure 1C and is consistent with prior research.

claim: TCRa deletion breakpoints in tumor-infiltrating T-cells were distributed over multiple genomic bins and not shared between cells.
source: In the purified CD4+/CD8+ T-cell nuclei (n = 95), deletion breakpoints were found distributed over 14 genomic bins and in the majority of T-cells were not shared, suggesting unique TCRa recombination events (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the breakpoint analysis shown in Figure 1D and supplementary figures.

claim: Within a given tumor, none of the T-cells shared identical TCRa deletion breakpoints, suggesting they were non-clonally derived and genetically distinct.
source: Extending this breakpoint analysis to T-cells identified in patient biopsies, we found that within a given tumor none of the T-cells shared identical breakpoints, similarly suggesting that the identified T-cells were non-clonally derived and genetically distinct.
evidence: This is based on the breakpoint analysis of T-cells found in tumor biopsies, with inference about clonality.

claim: T-cell leukemia nuclei showed recurrent and positionally identical TCRa deletion breakpoints across different single nuclei.
source: This is in contrast to the breakpoints observed in nuclei derived from a T-cell leukemia which were recurrent and positionally identical across different single nuclei (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the breakpoint analysis data shown in Figure 1D and supplementary figures.

claim: T-cell leukemia nuclei had lower breakpoint pairwise-distance values compared to CD8+/CD4+ T-cells and T-cells found in breast cancer biopsies.
source: Indeed, we find lower breakpoint pairwise-distance values in the single-nuclei derived from the T-cell leukemia compared to both CD8+/CD4+ T-cells and T-cells found in breast cancer biopsies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of breakpoint distances shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: All T-cell leukemia nuclei shared identical TCRa deletion breakpoints (p-value<10−6).
source: All the T-cell leukemia nuclei in this analysis shared identical breakpoints, p-value<10−6, in contrast to T-cells found in tumor biopsies.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the breakpoint data.

claim: Large karyotypic abnormalities were observed affecting some T-cell genomes.
source: In addition to the heterogeneity of the TCRa deletion breakpoints in T-cells, we observed large karyotypic abnormalities affecting some T-cell genomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the copy number profiles shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Karyotypic abnormalities in T-cells were represented overwhelmingly by loss of an entire copy of the X chromosome.
source: These karyotypic abnormalities were represented overwhelmingly by a loss of an entire copy of the X chromosome (Figure 1E) consistent with previous karyotyping studies of proliferating lymphocytes (Nowinski et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1E and is consistent with prior research.

claim: X-loss T-cells found in the same patient sample were genetically distinct at their respective TCRa locus.
source: These X-loss T-cells, when found in the same patient sample, were genetically distinct at their respective TCRa locus as judged by the deletion breakpoints as well as the above mentioned breakpoint-distance metric (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TCRa deletion breakpoints in X-loss T-cells.

claim: T-cells displaying X-loss were found more frequently in estrogen receptor negative (ER-) compared to estrogen receptor positive (ER+) tumors (p-value=0.0047).
source: Interestingly, T-cells displaying X-loss were found more frequently in estrogen receptor negative (ER-) compared to estrogen receptor positive (ER+) tumors (p-value=0.0047) (Figure 1E, insert).
evidence: This association is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: BRCA1 has been shown experimentally to be associated with the process of X-inactivation.
source: Given that BRCA1 has been shown experimentally to be associated with the process of X-inactivation (Ganesan et al., 2002) and that BRCA1-mutant tumors are mostly ER- tumors, this association is intriguing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: BRCA1-mutant tumors are mostly ER- tumors.
source: Given that BRCA1 has been shown experimentally to be associated with the process of X-inactivation (Ganesan et al., 2002) and that BRCA1-mutant tumors are mostly ER- tumors, this association is intriguing.
evidence: This represents established knowledge in breast cancer biology.

claim: Pseudo-diploid cells carry non-clonal, genetically heterogeneous CNAs.
source: Additionally, we and others have reported the detection of individual, aneuploid nuclei that carry non-clonal, genetically heterogeneous CNAs termed pseudo-diploids (Navin et al., 2011; Demeulemeester et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research by the authors and others.

claim: Pseudo-diploids were initially identified in two triple negative primary tumors and not their matching metastasis.
source: Initially identified in two triple negative primary tumors and not their matching metastasis (Navin et al., 2011), here, we extend their observation to tumors from all four PAM50 subtypes studied (i.e. LumA, LumB, HER2+, and Basal) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Pseudo-diploids were observed in tumors from all four PAM50 subtypes studied (LumA, LumB, HER2+, and Basal).
source: Initially identified in two triple negative primary tumors and not their matching metastasis (Navin et al., 2011), here, we extend their observation to tumors from all four PAM50 subtypes studied (i.e. LumA, LumB, HER2+, and Basal) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Some pseudo-diploid cells carry prototypical breast cancer CNAs such as gain of 1q and loss of 16p.
source: Interestingly, we find that some carry prototypical breast cancer CNAs such as gain of 1q and loss of 16 p (Figure 1F – right panel).
evidence: This is supported by the copy number profiles shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The pseudo-diploids observed do not appear to be precursors to the clonal cancer cells constituting the tumor mass.
source: The pseudo-diploids observed in our cohort however do not appear to be precursors to the clonal cancer cells constituting the tumor mass as they do not share their respective CNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on comparison of CNAs in pseudo-diploid cells versus cancer cells, shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Pseudo-diploid nuclei are interpreted as a manifestation of the inherent genomic instability present in normal breast epithelial cells of cancer patients.
source: We interpret the observation of these nuclei as a manifestation of the inherent genomic instability present in normal breast epithelial cells of cancer patients.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on the observed characteristics of pseudo-diploid cells.

claim: For tumor P5 (LumA), losses of 8p and 18p are clonal events.
source: For example, losses of 8 p and 18 p (recurrent CNAs in breast cancers) are found at one copy number state and are thus clonal events (Figure 2A – red arrows).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell copy number profiles shown in Figure 2A.

claim: For tumor P5 (LumA), gains at 1q and 8q as well as losses on chromosomes 13 and X are sub-clonal.
source: Alternatively, gains at 1q and 8q (also recurrent breast cancer CNAs) as well as losses on chromosomes 13 and X are found to be sub-clonal (Figure 2A – blue arrows).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell copy number profiles shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Tumor P5 is sub-clonal in over half of its genome (56% sub-clonal).
source: For P5, computing the fraction of the genome found to be clonal/sub-clonal using a stringent threshold (minimum 10% of cells showing sub-clonality – Materials and methods), we find P5 to be sub-clonal in over half of its genome (56% sub-clonal) (Figure 2A - top bar).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of the single-cell data for tumor P5.

claim: Tumors show a wide range of fractional sub-clonal values, with some showing significant (>40% genome sub-clonal), moderate (5-20% sub-clonal), or low levels (<5% sub-clonal) of heterogeneity.
source: Extending this analysis to all tumors, we find a wide range of fractional sub-clonal values with tumors showing: (1) significant (sub-clonal at ~>40% genome – Ex: P5, P22, and P59), (2) moderate (5%–20% subclonal-- Ex: P14, P58, and P31) or (3) low levels of heterogeneity (subclonal at <5% of genome – Ex: P16, P41, P1) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of sub-clonality across all tumor samples shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Sub-clonal CNAs affect regions recurrently altered in breast cancer genomes (e.g., 8p and 13q).
source: Importantly, regions found to be sub-clonal in tumor samples included regions: (1) known to be recurrently altered by CNAs (ex: 8 p and 13q)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C and represents integration with known breast cancer CNA patterns.

claim: Sub-clonal CNAs affect regions harboring genes encoding therapeutic targets such as ESR1, CYP19A, CDK6, and PD-L1.
source: (2) harboring genes encoding therapeutic targets such as ESR1, CYP19A (Ellis et al., 2012), CDK6 (Turner et al., 2015), and PD-L1 (Nanda et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D and citations to research on these therapeutic targets.

claim: Sub-clonal CNAs affect regions harboring genes known to be recurrently mutated by SNVs such as PIK3R1, PDGFRA, and RUNX1.
source: (3) harboring genes known to be recurrently mutated by single nucleotide variants (SNVs) such as PIK3R1, PDGFRA, and RUNX1 (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Nik-Zainal et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2E and citations to prior genomic studies.

claim: Sub-clonal CNAs affect regions harboring genes experimentally shown to be involved in metastasis.
source: (4) harboring genes experimentally shown to be involved in metastasis (Valiente et al., 2014; Wagenblast et al., 2015; Ross et al., 2015; Figure 2C - F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2F and citations to experimental studies on metastasis.

claim: Some sub-clonal CNAs exist at three or more distinct copy number states in different single cells.
source: Importantly, for some of the alterations, we find that the sub-clonal CNAs exist at three or more distinct copy number states in different single cells, for example, 8q gains in P5 (LumA) and P22 (Basal) (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the single-cell copy number data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: 1q/8q high tumors in ER+/HER2- patients are associated with worst distant relapse free survival.
source: Indeed, we find that 1q/8q high tumors in ER+/HER2- patients (regardless of ploidy status of the tumor genome) are associated with worst distant relapse free survival (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on survival analysis of METABRIC data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: 1q/8q high tumors are enriched in the IC9 subgroup which is associated with high-risk of late distant relapse.
source: Further, among the newly discovered breast cancer subgroups (IntClust, IC) groups, we find that 1q/8q high tumors are enriched in the IC9 subgroup which is associated with high-risk of late distant relapse (Rueda et al., 2019; Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of METABRIC data shown in the supplementary figure and citation to prior research.

claim: Prototypical driver amplifications containing ERBB2, CCND1, MYC, and CCNE1 were identified in the patient cohort.
source: Focal amplifications and deletions comprise another important class of CNAs. Prototypical driver amplifications containing ERBB2, CCND1, MYC, and CCNE1, as well as less commonly identified amplifications such as PPM1D and MDM2, were identified in our patient cohort and in some cases were clonal (i.e. identified in all single-nuclei sequenced) (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on the amplification data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Less commonly identified amplifications such as PPM1D and MDM2 were identified in the patient cohort.
source: Prototypical driver amplifications containing ERBB2, CCND1, MYC, and CCNE1, as well as less commonly identified amplifications such as PPM1D and MDM2, were identified in our patient cohort and in some cases were clonal (i.e. identified in all single-nuclei sequenced) (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on the amplification data shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: In tumor P22 (basal), three focal amplicons encompassing the VEGFA, MYC and CCNE1 loci were found in varying proportions.
source: For example in tumor P22 (basal), three focal amplicons encompassing the VEGFA, MYC and CCNE1 loci were found in varying proportions and in certain instances (VEGFA and CCNE1) in a mutually exclusive manner in sequenced single-nuclei (p-value=0.003 – Fisher's Exact Test).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell data from tumor P22 with statistical testing.

claim: In tumor P22, VEGFA and CCNE1 amplicons were found in a mutually exclusive manner (p-value=0.003).
source: For example in tumor P22 (basal), three focal amplicons encompassing the VEGFA, MYC and CCNE1 loci were found in varying proportions and in certain instances (VEGFA and CCNE1) in a mutually exclusive manner in sequenced single-nuclei (p-value=0.003 – Fisher's Exact Test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the co-occurrence of amplicons in single cells from tumor P22.

claim: In tumor P22, a sub-population lacking any amplicons but having lost an additional copy of the RB1 gene via a focal deletion was identified.
source: A sub-population lacking any of the amplicons, but having lost an additional copy of the RB1 gene via a focal deletion was also identified (Figure 3B and C and Figure 3 – figure supplement B-D).
evidence: This is based on single-cell copy number data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: In tumor P22, the amplifications segregate with genetically distinct, geographically resolved tumor sub-populations.
source: Interestingly, the amplifications segregate with genetically distinct, geographically resolved tumor sub-populations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering and DNA-FISH validation shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: In tumor P5 (LumA), an amplification targeting GATA6 was found only in a sub-population of cancer cells.
source: Other examples of amplicon mosaicism include P5 (LumA) where an amplification targeting GATA6 was found only in a sub-population of cancer cells
evidence: This is based on single-cell copy number data from tumor P5.

claim: In tumor P59 (Basal), amplifications on multiple chromosomes targeting genes such as LOX and PRDM1 were found in the majority of cells but absent in others.
source: and P59 (Basal), where amplifications on multiple chromosomes (chromosomes 3, 5, 6 and 18) targeting important genes such as LOX (Cox et al., 2015) and PRDM1 (Nik-Zainal et al., 2016) where found in the majority of cells but absent in others (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on single-cell copy number data shown in the supplementary figure and citations to prior research on these genes.

claim: 6 out of 16 (37%) tumors analyzed displayed amplicon mosaicism in the form of presence/absence of one or more amplicons in different subpopulations of cancer cells.
source: In total, 6 out of the 16 (37%) tumors analyzed displayed amplicon mosaicism in the form of presence/absence of one or more amplicons in different subpopulations of cancer cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the amplicon mosaicism observed across the cohort.

claim: In tumor P6 (HER2+), different spatially resolved sub-populations were identified carrying either only ERBB2 amplification, ERBB2 and SKIL amplifications, or ERBB2, SKIL, and MYC amplifications.
source: An example is P6 (HER2+) where different spatially resolved sub-populations were identified carrying either: (1) only ERBB2 amplification, (2) ERBB2 and SKIL amplifications, or (3) ERBB2, SKIL, and MYC amplifications (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is based on single-cell copy number data and DNA-FISH validation shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: For the SKIL and MYC amplicons in tumor P6, different single-nuclei were found to have varying levels/dosage of amplification.
source: Importantly, for the SKIL and MYC amplicons, different single-nuclei were found to have varying levels/dosage of amplification. Where in some single-nuclei, SKIL and MYC levels reached over 60 copies, in others the level of amplification was less pronounced.
evidence: This is based on analysis of copy number levels in single cells from tumor P6.

claim: In tumor P6, certain subpopulations contained MYC amplifications at less than 30 copies.
source: For the MYC locus for example certain subpopulations contained MYC amplifications at less than 30 copies (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on single-cell copy number data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Heterogeneity in SKIL and MYC amplicon level/dosage in tumor P6 was confirmed using DNA-FISH analysis based on fluorescence signal intensity.
source: This was confirmed using DNA-FISH analysis based on fluorescence signal intensity (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is based on DNA-FISH validation shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Heterogeneity in amplicon level/dosage was also observed for the ERBB2 locus in another HER2 amplified tumor.
source: This heterogeneity in amplicon level/dosage was also observed for the ERBB2 locus in another one of the six HER2 amplified tumors we analyzed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is based on single-cell and DNA-FISH data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: Homozygous deletions affecting known breast cancer genes such as MLLT4, MAP2K2, and NCoR1 were observed.
source: We also observed homozygous deletions affecting known breast cancer genes such as MLLT4, MAP2K2, and NCoR1, among others (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Nik-Zainal et al., 2016; Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on the deletion data shown in the supplementary figure and citations to prior genomic studies.

claim: No heterogeneity was observed in homozygous deletions.
source: However, we did not observe heterogeneity in this class of CNAs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of homozygous deletions across the single-cell data.

claim: For 9 of the 16 tumors analyzed, bulk DNA from two spatially resolved biopsies was sequenced and compared for CNAs.
source: For 9 of the 16 tumors analyzed, we were able to sequence and compare bulk DNA from two spatially resolved biopsies for CNAs.
evidence: This describes the multi-region sampling performed in the study.

claim: Substantial differences in CNAs were found between spatially resolved biopsies.
source: In concordance with previous studies, we find substantial differences in CNAs between biopsies (Yates et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on comparison of bulk copy number profiles and is consistent with prior research.

claim: Much of the variation observed between two biopsies can also be observed as sub-clonal variation in the single-cell data.
source: Interestingly however, we find that much of the variation observed between the two biopsies can also be observed as sub-clonal variation in the single-cell data (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of bulk and single-cell copy number data shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claim: Of 54 alterations differentially found in two analyzed biopsies from nine patients, 35 (65%) were identified in the single-cell data.
source: Of 54 alterations differentially found in the two analyzed biopsies from the nine patients, 35 (65%) were identified in the data from single nuclei.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the overlap between multi-region and single-cell data.

claim: Additional heterogeneous CNAs were detected only in the single-cell data and not in the bulk comparisons.
source: Importantly, additional heterogeneous CNAs were detected only in the single-cell data and not in the bulk comparisons, for example variation on chromosome 1q and 1 p in P22 as well as alterations on 1q and chromosome four in P5, with the converse also being true (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of bulk and single-cell copy number data.

claim: Polyploid tumors are significantly more likely to be heterogeneous on the copy number level (p-value=0.0164).
source: (2) Polyploid tumors are significantly more likely to be heterogeneous on the copy number level and this relationship is unrelated to the total number of clonal alterations found in each tumor.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A using Wilcoxon rank order testing.

claim: ER- tumors are significantly more heterogeneous on the copy number level than ER+ tumors (p-value=0.0229).
source: (3) As a group ER- tumors are significantly more heterogeneous on the copy number level than ER+ tumors.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A using Wilcoxon rank order testing.

claim: Tumor P5, an ER+/LumA tumor with extensive copy number and clonal heterogeneity, is mutated for the TP53 gene.
source: There is one exceptional outlier, an ER+/LumA (P5) with extensive copy number and clonal heterogeneity. Interestingly, unlike most ER+ tumors, P5 is mutated for the TP53 gene (Figure 5B), as are the majority of ER- tumors.
evidence: This is based on Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In ER+ tumors (excluding the ER+/TP53 mutant case), tumor size and CNA heterogeneity are inversely correlated (p-value=0.02793).
source: However, when restricting the analysis to ER+ tumors (and excluding the ER+/TP53 mutated case) we find a relationship where tumor size and CNA heterogeneity are inversely correlated (p-value=0.02793).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The largest four tumors (measuring at more than 10 cm2) display the least amount of CNA heterogeneity.
source: The largest four tumors (measuring at more than 10 cm2) display the least amount of CNA heterogeneity (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of tumor size and heterogeneity data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Tumor samples conform to three different clonal classes: homogenous tumors with a single clone, heterogeneous tumors with multiple clones but one dominant, and heterogeneous tumors with many clones and none dominant.
source: Lastly, we examined the clonal composition of cancer cells from analyzed tumor samples (i.e. # of genetically distinct clones in a given sample and their relative frequencies) and find that tumor samples in general conform to three different clonal classes: (1) homogenous tumors where only a single clone is observed, found only in ER+ tumors; (2) heterogeneous tumors where multiple clones exist but with one clone dominant over others (i.e. dominant >50%), a pattern found throughout the cohort subtypes; and (3) heterogeneous tumors where many clones are found at varying frequencies with none of them being dominant, mainly in ER- tumors (Figure 5E and F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on clonal composition analysis shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Homogenous tumors with a single clone were found only in ER+ tumors.
source: (1) homogenous tumors where only a single clone is observed, found only in ER+ tumors
evidence: This is based on clonal composition analysis across the cohort.

claim: Heterogeneous tumors with many clones and none dominant were mainly found in ER- tumors.
source: (3) heterogeneous tumors where many clones are found at varying frequencies with none of them being dominant, mainly in ER- tumors
evidence: This is based on clonal composition analysis across the cohort.

claim: Pseudo-diploid single cells were observed in the majority of studied tumors across different PAM50 subtypes.
source: Second, we observe pseudo-diploid single cells in the majority of our studied tumors, across different PAM50 subtypes, providing further evidence for the existence of such cells in breast cancer tissue.
evidence: This is based on the data presented in Figure 1C and related analyses.

claim: Cancer-specific alterations (e.g. 1q gain and 16q loss) were observed in pseudo-diploid cells.
source: This, coupled with the observation of cancer-specific alterations (e.g. 1q gain and 16q loss) in these cells raises the question of whether these cells are a manifestation of the intrinsic genomic instability of the mammary epithelial cells of breast cancer patients and whether their detection might be useful in early stage risk assessment.
evidence: This is based on the data shown in Figure 1F and represents an observation with speculative implications.

claim: Profound genetic heterogeneity in CNAs affects genes and regions with known biological relevance in breast cancer.
source: Third, we observe profound genetic heterogeneity in CNAs affecting genes and regions with known biological relevance in breast cancer, such as genes associated with metastasis and therapeutic response.
evidence: This is based on the data presented in Figure 2C-F showing sub-clonal CNAs affecting important genes.

claim: CNAs can be found at different copy numbers in different populations of cells.
source: Fourth, we find that CNA heterogeneity is not binary (i.e. sub-clonal or clonal). CNAs can be found at different copy numbers in different populations of cells and that this, in the case of 1q/8q gains is associated with clinical outcome, likely a consequence of dosage dependent biology.
evidence: This is based on the data shown in Figure 2G and survival analysis in Figure 2H.

claim: Different levels of 1q/8q gains are associated with clinical outcome.
source: CNAs can be found at different copy numbers in different populations of cells and that this, in the case of 1q/8q gains is associated with clinical outcome, likely a consequence of dosage dependent biology.

claim: Mosaicism in recurrent driver amplicons was observed in a significant proportion of tumors.
source: Fifth, the observation of mosaicism in recurrent driver amplicons in a significant proportion of tumors has clinical implications given that driver amplicon genes are often targets for drug development (e.g., ERBB2, MET, and EGFR) and have been proposed to be good targets for drug development in breast cancer (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012).
evidence: This is based on the amplicon heterogeneity data presented in Figure 3 and related analyses.

source: Further, we find additional layers of heterogeneity in this class of CNAs: the presence or absence of an amplicon and variation in the level/dosage of amplification, which might be the result of extra-chromosomal amplicon instability (Turner et al., 2017).

source: Eight, the association of CNA heterogeneity with parameters such as polyploidy and ER- status provides an indirect association of heterogeneity with clinical outcome since both parameters have been shown to associate with a worse prognosis (Carey et al., 2006; Pinto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the associations found in the study and citations to prior research on prognosis.

source: Similarly the observation that CNAs can be found at more than two distinct copy number states, which we show is associated with clinical outcome, and the identification of somatic amplicon mosaicism in a substantial proportion of breast cancer biopsies is the result of the single-cell resolution of the data and importantly, has been missed by many prior bulk genomic studies.
